body_markdown:
A popular gourmet popcorn product has been placed under a serious food safety recall after concerns about possible Salmonella contamination.


The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has classified the recall involving Coco G's Gourmet Flaming Cheddar Hots popcorn as a Class I recall, the agency's highest level of recall classification. The action involves a limited quantity of popcorn distributed in Wisconsin and Illinois.


The recall highlights why consumers should pay close attention to product names, package sizes, lot numbers and expiration dates when federal health officials announce a food safety alert.


## Coco G's Popcorn Recall Involves Salmonella Concern


According to information provided in the FDA enforcement alert, Coco G's Snack Food of Union Grove, Wisconsin, withdrew 270 bags of Gourmet Flaming Cheddar Hots popcorn from the market.


The products were removed from shelves on May 5 following concerns about possible Salmonella contamination.


The affected products include specific plastic bags sold in several package sizes. Consumers who may have purchased the popcorn should check their packaging carefully rather than assuming that every Coco G's popcorn product is included in the recall.


The recalled products identified in the enforcement information include:


- 2.5-ounce bags with UPC 6 94161-25911 9
- 4.15-ounce bags with UPC 6 94161-38911 3
- 5-ounce bags with UPC 6 94161-60005 8
- Lot code 007560
- Expiration date of June 10


Other Gourmet Flaming Cheddar Hots varieties are not included in the recall information described here. Those products include Caramel & Cheddar Cheese, Caramel Corn and Wisconsin Cheddar.


Consumers should rely on the specific product identifiers listed by the FDA rather than assuming that every popcorn product from the company is affected.


## What Does a Class I Recall Mean?


The FDA uses three recall classifications to indicate the relative level of health hazard associated with a recalled product.


A Class I recall represents the highest level of concern. The FDA defines it as a situation in which there is a reasonable probability that use of or exposure to a violative product could result in serious adverse health consequences or death.


That classification does not mean that every person who consumed the recalled food will become seriously ill. Instead, it indicates the level of potential risk identified by the FDA when evaluating the product.


The FDA also uses Class II and Class III classifications. Class II recalls involve products that could cause temporary or medically reversible health consequences, while Class III recalls involve situations where adverse health consequences are not likely.


The agency notes that recall classifications can be assigned after companies provide information needed to evaluate the public health risk. Therefore, the classification reflects the FDA's assessment of the recall situation and should be considered alongside the specific product information and instructions issued by the agency.


## Why Salmonella Is a Food Safety Concern


Salmonella is a type of bacteria that can cause an illness known as salmonellosis. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, common symptoms include diarrhea, fever and stomach cramps. Nausea, vomiting and headaches can also occur.


Symptoms can begin within several hours to several days after exposure. Many people recover within several days, but Salmonella infections can sometimes lead to complications.


The CDC says certain people have a higher risk of serious illness, including young children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems.


Consumers who experience severe symptoms after eating a recalled product should seek medical advice. Warning signs can include bloody diarrhea, prolonged diarrhea, high fever, repeated vomiting or symptoms of dehydration.


## What Consumers Should Do


Anyone who believes they have one of the recalled popcorn products should avoid eating it.


Check the product name, package size, UPC number, lot code and expiration information against the details provided in the recall notice.


If the package matches the recalled information, consumers should follow the instructions provided by the company or FDA regarding disposal or return. Keeping the packaging can also be useful because product information may help identify exactly what was purchased.


Consumers who believe they became sick after consuming a recalled food should consider speaking with a healthcare professional. The CDC recommends keeping track of foods eaten and discussing possible foodborne illness with a healthcare provider when appropriate.


## Another Popcorn Recall Involved Labeling Issues


The Coco G's recall is not the only recent popcorn-related enforcement action.


In a separate recall, Prospector Popcorn of Ridgefield, Connecticut, withdrew several gourmet popcorn products because of inaccurately declared nutrient information.


The affected products included Chocolate Mocha Gourmet Popcorn, Maple Walnut Ice Cream Gourmet Popcorn, Fudge Brownie Gourmet Popcorn and Belgian Chocolate Toffee Gourmet Popcorn.


According to the information supplied for that recall, approximately 21,400 bags distributed across 43 states and the District of Columbia were involved.


The issue was different from the Coco G's recall. Prospector Popcorn management stated that the recall concerned a labeling error and was not caused by contamination, an undeclared allergen or a product defect.


Federal officials identified discrepancies involving nutrients such as carbohydrates, cholesterol, potassium, calcium, iron and vitamin D, depending on the product.


This distinction is important because not every food recall means that the food itself is contaminated. Some recalls involve packaging problems, labeling errors or other regulatory issues.


## Why Checking Food Recalls Matters


Food recalls can involve products ranging from snacks and beverages to meat, dairy products and packaged foods.


Consumers may not always realize that a product in their pantry is subject to a recall, particularly when only certain lot numbers or package sizes are affected.


Checking the FDA's recall information can help consumers determine whether a particular item is included. The agency's Enforcement Report contains recall information and identifies the classification assigned to products subject to FDA-monitored recalls.


The most important detail is to match the exact product information. A recall affecting one flavor, size or lot does not automatically mean that every product made by the same company is affected.


For the Coco G's popcorn recall, consumers should pay particular attention to the product name, UPC, lot code and expiration information.


## Bottom Line


The FDA's Class I classification makes the Coco G's Gourmet Flaming Cheddar Hots recall a significant food safety matter. The recall concerns specific popcorn products associated with a potential Salmonella contamination issue.


Consumers who have the affected product should not eat it and should check the official recall information for instructions.


The situation also demonstrates why consumers should distinguish between different types of recalls. A Class I food recall associated with potential contamination carries a different risk profile from a recall caused by a labeling mistake.


When a food recall is announced, checking the exact product identifiers and following instructions from federal officials and the manufacturer can help consumers make informed decisions about products in their homes.
